newsitem.title: GERMANY: German employer group demands change to strike law.
newsitem.headline: German employer group demands change to strike law.

text.p: A major German employers' federation, the Gesamtmetal, called on Monday for new laws that would curb the power of trade unions after suffering a setback in regional talks over sick pay last week. Werner Stumpfe, head of the federation of German metal and engineering employers, said the laws should make industrial action including all-out strikes by workers more difficult.
"We need alternatives so that strikes, as a means of industrial action that damages companies and jobs, are no longer required," Stumpfe said on German radio.
Gesamtmetal said on Sunday resistance by metal and engineering workers had made a new law cutting sick pay costs unenforceable in the sector.
German industrial relations have plummeted to new lows since the introduction of the law in October, cutting sick payments from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

In reference to a dispute that has included walk-outs by hundreds of thousands of German engineering workers over the past two months, Stumpfe said labour law needed to be changed "so that we don't have to fight each other like Neandertals".
Under clauses in metal and engineering wage contracts, workers are not allowed to strike until after a four-week "cooling off" period following the termination of existing contracts.

This has not however stopped them downing tools for up to a day at a time in protests that have cost firms such as Daimler-Benz AG's Mercedes car-making unit tens of millions of marks in lost production.

With the IG Metall union -- the world's largest trade union with nearly three million members -- warning of all-out strikes next year, employers in the sector have started to back down on implementing the sick pay law.
Gesamtmetall acknowledged on Sunday it would have to live with a regional wage deal signed in the sector last week that did not implement the sick pay law.
Stumpfe said that although the deal in the northern state of Lower Saxony was "very disappointing", it accepted that it would now likely set the tone for settlements in other regions.
Employers in part of the southern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg are expected to be the next in the industry to sign 1997 wage deals guaranteeing full sick payments for some 300,000 workers.
IG Metall has hailed the retreat by employers as a victory for the industrial action carried out by the workers.

Other industries such as the much smaller confectionery sector are already facing strikes because wage contracts there do not require the cooling-off period which is mandatory in the metal and engineering branches.
The German unit of Swiss food giant Nestle SA on Sunday became the latest producer in the sector to back down on the sick pay cuts after strikes at its Hamburg and Berlin plants.
